title: Life Assurance Underwriting: Principles and Best Practices

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the concept of anti-selection in life assurance underwriting?

opts.x: The tendency of insurers to select only the healthiest applicants for coverage.
The tendency of high-risk individuals to disproportionately seek or increase insurance coverage compared to low-risk individuals.
The practice of applying exclusion clauses to all policies regardless of individual health status.
A regulatory requirement under NIIRA 2025 for insurers to decline high-risk occupational classes.

questions.answer: (B) The tendency of high-risk individuals to disproportionately seek or increase insurance coverage compared to low-risk individuals.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Anti-selection (also called adverse selection) describes the phenomenon whereby those who have the most to gain from insurance are more likely to seek it, and to seek higher amounts of it, than those with lower risk profiles. If a person knows they have an elevated risk of dying (through illness, family history, or lifestyle) they have a stronger financial incentive to secure large life cover. If insurers cannot adequately identify and price this elevated risk, they end up insuring a disproportionately high-risk pool, which drives claims above the level priced into premiums. Anti-selection is the primary reason underwriting exists: it is the mechanism that identifies and prices the elevated risk before it enters the pool.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) describes the insurer's selection process; the act of assessing and accepting or declining risks. Anti-selection is the market dynamic that motivates that selection process, not the process itself.

(C) describes a broad exclusion underwriting approach, a specific underwriting decision tool. This is not the definition of anti-selection.

(D) There is no NIIRA 2025 requirement to automatically decline high-risk occupational classes. NIIRA 2025 requires individualised risk assessment; blanket occupational declines would be inconsistent with its consumer protection provisions.

questions.stem: A Non-Medical Limit (NML) in life assurance underwriting is best defined as:

opts.x: The maximum sum assured an insurer will offer under any circumstances.
The sum assured above which an insurer requires the applicant to undergo a medical examination.
The minimum sum assured below which no underwriting assessment is required.
The limit above which NAICOM requires regulatory approval.

questions.answer: (B) The sum assured above which an insurer requires the applicant to undergo a medical examination.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The NML is an underwriting threshold set by each insurer: applications for sums assured at or below the NML may be accepted on the basis of the proposal form alone (non-medical basis), without requiring a formal medical examination. Once the proposed sum assured exceeds the NML, the insurer requires medical evidence, at minimum a medical examination report (MER) from a GP, and for very large sums assured, specialist cardiac investigations, blood profiles, and HIV tests. The NML varies by insurer and is calibrated by age: younger applicants typically qualify for higher non-medical limits.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The NML is not an absolute cap on the sum assured an insurer will offer; it is a threshold above which additional evidence is required. There is no fixed maximum; very large sums assured (₦500m+) may be accepted at appropriate terms with sufficient medical and financial evidence.

(C) Inverts the definition. Below the NML, applications can proceed without a medical examination. Above the NML, a medical is required.

(D) NAICOM does not require regulatory approval for individual large-sum policies. The NML is a purely internal underwriting tool.

questions.stem: An applicant discloses a pre-existing lower back condition for which they receive physiotherapy. The insurer issues the policy at standard premium rates but excludes claims arising from the back condition. This decision is called:

opts.x: A flat extra premium loading.
A postponement.
A declination.
An exclusion.

why.h: Why (D) is Correct

An exclusion is an underwriting decision that accepts the applicant at standard premium rates but removes specific conditions or causes of death from coverage. The insurer takes the view that the applicant's overall mortality risk is standard, the back condition does not materially shorten life expectancy, but that claims directly caused by the back condition should not be insured because the risk is not adequately priced at standard rates. The exclusion clause is appended to the policy and is binding.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) A flat extra premium loading accepts the policy for all causes of death (no exclusion) but charges an additional premium per thousand sum assured to reflect the elevated overall mortality risk. Used when the elevated risk applies to all causes, not to one specific condition.

(B) A postponement defers the underwriting decision, the insurer declines to accept the application now but invites the applicant to reapply after a defined period (e.g., after recovery from recent surgery or after a waiting period following a cancer diagnosis). No cover is issued.

(C) A declination is an outright refusal to offer insurance at all, on any terms. This is the most severe underwriting outcome and is reserved for risks that are completely unacceptable even with loadings or exclusions.

questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025, an insurer's response to an application from an HIV-positive individual must:

opts.x: Automatically decline the application.
Issue the policy at standard terms as no loading is permitted.
Conduct an individualised assessment based on current clinical status and not decline solely on HIV-positive status.
Refer all HIV-positive applications to NAICOM for approval.

questions.answer: (C) Conduct an individualised assessment based on the applicant's current clinical status and not decline solely on the basis of HIV-positive status.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 prohibits discriminatory automatic declinations based on protected health status. An insurer confronted with an HIV-positive applicant must assess the individual's current clinical position: CD4 count and trend; viral load (detectable or undetectable on ART); adherence to antiretroviral therapy; presence of opportunistic infections or AIDS-defining conditions; overall health profile. An applicant with well-controlled HIV on ART, undetectable viral load, and a high CD4 count has a materially different mortality profile from one with advanced AIDS. Blanket automatic declination ignores this clinical reality and violates NIIRA 2025's individualised assessment requirement.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Automatic declination based solely on HIV-positive status is discriminatory and contrary to NIIRA 2025. The insurer may ultimately decline after individualized assessment if the clinical picture warrants it, but the declination must be based on assessed risk, not status alone.

(B) Standard terms without any loading may not be appropriate, well-controlled HIV still carries somewhat elevated mortality compared to the general population, particularly in Nigeria where healthcare access may be inconsistent. The insurer may appropriately apply a premium loading or benefit modification.

(D) NAICOM does not require application-by-application approval for HIV-positive cases. The insurer applies its own underwriting framework within NIIRA 2025's principles.

questions.stem: Moratorium underwriting, as applied in Nigerian group life schemes, means:

opts.x: The insurer delays its underwriting decision while collecting medical evidence.
Individual medical evidence is waived for all group members, but claims from pre-existing conditions within a defined exclusion period are not covered.
The insurer issues all policies at standard rates without any exclusions or loadings.
NAICOM authorises the scheme under a special regulatory moratorium.

questions.answer: (B) Individual medical evidence is waived for all group members, but claims from pre-existing conditions within a defined exclusion period are not covered.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Moratorium underwriting is a group underwriting approach that balances operational efficiency with anti-selection protection. All eligible employees join the scheme automatically, no individual medical evidence is collected. In exchange, any claim arising from a condition that existed before the member joined the scheme (or within the moratorium period, typically 1–2 years) is excluded. The exclusion window prevents an employee who knows they are seriously ill from joining the group scheme immediately before making a claim. After the moratorium period, all conditions are covered, including pre-existing ones.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) describes a postponement, deferring the underwriting decision while evidence is gathered. Moratorium underwriting does not delay the decision; it makes an immediate acceptance decision, but with a built-in pre-existing condition exclusion.

(C) Standard rates without any exclusions describe full medical underwriting at standard terms; the most favourable outcome for the applicant. Moratorium underwriting is an intermediate position: automatic acceptance but with a time-limited exclusion.

(D) NAICOM does not issue special regulatory moratoriums for group schemes. Moratorium underwriting is a commercial underwriting approach, not a regulatory authorisation.

questions.stem:
A proposed life assured aged 48 has declared: controlled Type 2 diabetes (diagnosed 5 years ago, HbA1c currently 7.1%, on oral medication, no complications); BMI of 32; occupation as a long-distance lorry driver; and a family history of cardiovascular disease (father died of a heart attack at age 58). The proposed sum assured of ₦30 million exceeds the insurer’s NML of ₦20 million.
(a) Identify all the underwriting risk factors present in this case and classify each by significance.
(b) Describe the medical evidence you would request.
(c) Explain the range of special terms that might be applied and the basis for each.
(d) At what point, if any, would you refer this case to the reinsurer?

model.h: Part (a): Risk Factors and Classification

rows: MODERATE-HIGH. Controlled diabetes with HbA1c in the acceptable range but not optimal (<7.0%). Carries elevated cardiovascular and renal mortality risk. Duration 5 years is relevant, longer duration increases complication risk.
MODERATE. BMI 30–34 carries an excess mortality loading of approximately 25–50% above standard, primarily through cardiovascular and metabolic pathways. Compounds the diabetes risk.

MODERATE-HIGH. Elevated occupational hazard class, road traffic accident risk, irregular health monitoring, sedentary nature exacerbating metabolic risks, potential for fatigue-related incidents. Many Nigerian life insurers classify HGV drivers at Class 3 occupational risk.
MODERATE. Paternal cardiovascular death before age 60 is a recognised additional mortality loading. Compounds existing diabetes and BMI risks through shared genetic and lifestyle pathways.
TRIGGERS MEDICAL EVIDENCE. The excess ₦10m above the NML requires full medical examination regardless of the risk profile.

model.h: Part (b): Medical Evidence Required

Standard medical examination report (MER) by an approved GP: full physical examination including blood pressure measurement (critical given diabetes + BMI + family CVD history); current medication confirmation.

Blood investigations: HbA1c (current control, the declared 7.1% needs verification); fasting blood glucose; full lipid profile (cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, elevated in diabetics); renal function (eGFR, creatinine, diabetes affects kidneys); liver function tests.

Cardiovascular investigations: resting ECG (mandatory given age 48, diabetes, BMI 32, family CVD history). Stress ECG or echocardiogram if resting ECG shows any abnormality.

Urinalysis: microalbuminuria (early marker of diabetic nephropathy, a complication indicator even with 'no complications' declared).

HIV test: standard for sums assured exceeding the insurer's HIV NML (typically ₦10–20m in Nigeria).
Part (c): Range of Special Terms

The underwriter has several options depending on the medical evidence received:

1. Standard terms: Unlikely given the combination of risk factors, but possible if all investigations return clearly normal results and HbA1c is confirmed well-controlled.

2. Flat extra premium loading: Adding ₦2–₦5 per ₦1,000 sum assured to reflect excess mortality from the combination of diabetes, BMI, and occupational risk. This is the most commercially constructive outcome, the applicant pays more but receives full coverage.

3. Deferred decision (postponement): If investigations reveal a newly identified complication (proteinuria, ECG changes suggesting ischaemia), the underwriter may postpone acceptance for 12 months pending stabilisation.

4. Exclusion: Exclusion of cardiovascular-related claims would be considered, but is commercially problematic at this age, it removes the most probable cause of death and renders the policy of limited value. Most underwriters would prefer a premium loading to an exclusion for this risk profile.

5. Combination: Loading + occupational exclusion for accidents arising from HGV driving if the insurer wants to specifically limit road accident risk.
Part (d): Reinsurer Referral

Reinsurer referral is appropriate in two circumstances:

1. Sum assured exceeds the insurer's facultative reinsurance threshold: If the insurer's automatic acceptance limit for the relevant risk category (a rated, non-standard, age-48 life) is below ₦30m, the entire risk or the excess above the retention must be referred to the reinsurer for facultative acceptance before a decision is communicated to the proposer.

2. Complexity of the medical picture: If the cardiovascular investigations reveal unexpected findings (ECG abnormalities, significant proteinuria), this case (combining diabetes, CVD risk factors, occupational risk, and a large sum assured) warrants reinsurer input. Major reinsurers (Hannover Re, Swiss Re, Africa Re) provide technical underwriting support for complex cases as part of their treaty relationships.

questions.stem: Explain the financial underwriting process for individual life assurance in Nigeria. In your answer, define insurable interest and describe the categories of relationship in which it exists; explain the concept of income multiples and how they are applied; describe three red-flag indicators that would trigger an AML investigation during underwriting; and explain the regulatory framework under which the insurer’s AML obligations in the underwriting process arise.

model.h: Insurable Interest: Definition and Categories

Insurable interest is the legal and financial relationship between the policyholder and the life assured that justifies the policy's existence. Without insurable interest, a life policy would be a wagering contract on another person's life, void at law and socially harmful. Categories in Nigerian life assurance:

1. Own life: A person has unlimited insurable interest in their own life, no quantification required.

2. Spouse: A spouse has unlimited insurable interest in their spouse's life by virtue of the marital relationship, no financial dependency needs to be proved.

3. Children/dependants: A parent has unlimited interest in minor children's lives. For adult children, interest must be supported by financial dependency.

4. Business relationships, creditor/debtor: A creditor has insurable interest in a debtor's life limited to the amount of the outstanding debt. A bank taking out credit life insurance on a borrower's life has interest limited to the loan balance.

5. Business partners: Partners in a business have insurable interest in each other's lives to the extent of the financial loss the surviving partner would suffer, keyman insurance.

6. Employers: An employer has insurable interest in a key employee's life to the extent of the financial loss the business would suffer from that employee's death.
Income Multiples: Concept and Application

Income multiples are the financial underwriting tool used to assess whether the proposed sum assured is proportionate to the applicant's financial exposure, preventing over-insurance.

Typical Nigerian market income multiples by age:
• Under 40: up to 20× gross annual income
• 40–49: up to 15× gross annual income
• 50–55: up to 10× gross annual income
• 56–60: up to 7× gross annual income

Application: An applicant aged 42 declares gross annual income of ₦6,000,000. Maximum acceptable sum assured: 15 × ₦6,000,000 = ₦90,000,000. If the proposed sum assured is ₦120,000,000, the underwriter must either reduce the sum assured to ₦90m or request evidence of additional financial need (outstanding mortgage, business debt, key person loss) justifying the higher amount.

Limitation in the Nigerian informal economy: Income multiples require verifiable declared income. For self-employed applicants, informal traders, or those without tax returns, income verification is challenging. Underwriters must use alternative evidence: bank statements, business accounts, property ownership, lifestyle markers.
Three AML Red-Flag Indicators During Underwriting

1. Premium source inconsistency: The proposed sum assured and premium are disproportionate to the declared income and verifiable wealth. An applicant declaring an annual income of ₦3,000,000 proposing a ₦50m policy with a ₦1.2m annual premium, 40% of declared income, without any documented financial justification is a red flag for money laundering (using insurance to place and layer illicit funds).

2. Third-party premium payer with no clear relationship: A premium is proposed to be paid by a third party with no documented insurable interest or commercial relationship with the life assured. Legitimate business cases exist (employer-paid key person insurance) but must be fully documented. An unexplained third-party payer financing a large individual life policy is a classic red flag.

3. Unusual beneficiary arrangements: The named beneficiary is an entity (company, trust) rather than a family member, or is located in a high-risk jurisdiction, or is changed multiple times at inception without clear explanation. Complex beneficiary layering, multiple entities or jurisdictions in the payment chain, is a common money laundering indicator in life insurance globally.
AML Regulatory Framework

The insurer's AML obligations in the underwriting process arise from:

1. Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022 (MLPPA 2022): Designates life insurers as 'financial institutions' subject to AML/CFT obligations. Requires customer due diligence (CDD) at onboarding; enhanced due diligence (EDD) for high-risk applicants; ongoing monitoring; and Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) filing with the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU) for suspicious transactions.

2. NAICOM AML/CFT Guidelines: Provide sector-specific implementation guidance, including income thresholds that trigger EDD in life insurance underwriting.

3. NIIRA 2025: Reinforces the AML framework within the insurance regulatory structure and requires Boards to maintain AML compliance programmes.

In practice: Every large-sum life application (typically above ₦50m, or any application with red flags regardless of size) should trigger an EDD review: source of funds verification; politically exposed person (PEP) screening; adverse media search; UBO (ultimate beneficial owner) identification for company-linked applications.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer operates a group life scheme covering 5,000 employees of a large industrial company. The employer requires that all employees be covered regardless of health status. The insurer has elected to use moratorium underwriting.
(a) Explain how moratorium underwriting works in this context, including the terms that must be disclosed to covered members.
(b) Explain the underwriting risk the insurer assumes under this approach, and the measures it should take to manage that risk.
(c) Describe the circumstances under which a death claim on this scheme would be declined under the moratorium terms, and explain what the insurer must do to ensure the moratorium clause is enforceable under NIIRA 2025.

model.h: Part (a): How Moratorium Underwriting Works and Disclosure Requirements

Operation: Under the moratorium approach, every eligible employee is automatically enrolled from the scheme's commencement date (or from their employment start date for new joiners) without any individual medical questionnaire or examination. There is no individual underwriting assessment. In exchange, the scheme terms include a moratorium exclusion clause: any death claim arising from a condition that existed before the member's scheme entry date, or that first manifested within the moratorium period (typically the first 12–24 months of membership), is excluded from coverage.

After the moratorium period, all conditions, including those that existed at entry, are covered. The moratorium is effectively a time-limited waiting period for pre-existing condition coverage.

Required disclosures to covered members:
• The existence of the moratorium period and its duration (12 or 24 months, which the insurer has set).
• The definition of 'pre-existing condition' as used in the moratorium clause.
• The claims investigation process that will apply to deaths occurring within the moratorium period.
• Under NIIRA 2025, the disclosure must be in plain language and delivered to each member in writing (electronic delivery acceptable with confirmation of receipt) within 30 days of the scheme commencement.
Part (b): Underwriting Risk Assumed and Management Measures

Risk assumed: The insurer accepts the mortality risk of 5,000 employees without knowing the health profile of any individual. The moratorium exclusion provides protection only for pre-existing conditions within the defined period; the insurer is exposed to all genuinely new conditions arising after entry, and to any pre-existing conditions where causation cannot be established after the moratorium period.

Anti-selection risk: Despite the moratorium, employees who know they are seriously ill may accelerate their employment with the company specifically to access the group life coverage. For large industrial companies, this is a real but manageable risk.

Management measures:
1. Pricing: The premium rate must include a loading for the moratorium risk; the group is priced assuming a proportion of members will have undisclosed conditions that will generate early claims within the moratorium window.
2. Claims investigation protocol: Every death claim within the moratorium period must be investigated (death certificate, hospital records, GP notes, prior treatment history) to assess whether the cause of death is causally linked to a pre-existing condition.
3. FCL monitoring: The insurer may impose an FCL even under moratorium underwriting for the highest sum assured employees; those with entitlements significantly above average are separately risk-assessed.
4. Annual scheme review: At each annual renewal, actual mortality experience vs expected is reviewed. If claims frequency significantly exceeds pricing assumptions, the underwriter may increase rates, tighten the moratorium period, or impose additional underwriting requirements.
Part (c): Grounds for Declining a Moratorium Claim and NIIRA 2025 Enforceability

Circumstances for declining: A death claim is declinable under the moratorium terms if, and only if, the insurer can demonstrate, on the balance of probabilities, that:
(i) The deceased had a defined pre-existing condition before scheme entry or within the moratorium period; AND
(ii) The cause of death is causally linked to that pre-existing condition.

Both elements must be established. The mere existence of a prior condition is insufficient; the insurer must connect it to the cause of death.

NIIRA 2025 enforceability requirements: For the moratorium clause to be enforceable under NIIRA 2025:
1. The clause must have been clearly disclosed to the covered member (see Part (a)), a clause the member never received in plain language is vulnerable to contra proferentem challenge.
2. The decision to decline must be supported by documented investigation findings, not mere assertion.
3. The member (or their beneficiary) must be notified of the decline in writing with clear reasons and must be informed of their right to appeal to NAICOM's Consumer Protection Bureau within the specified period.
4. The insurer cannot rely on the moratorium clause to decline a claim where it cannot demonstrate the causal link between the pre-existing condition and the cause of death. If the member died of unrelated causes (e.g., a road accident), the moratorium clause cannot be used as a basis for declining; the death is not causally linked to any pre-existing condition.

questions.stem: Critically evaluate the effectiveness of the financial underwriting function as both a risk control mechanism and an AML/CFT compliance mechanism in Nigerian life assurance practice. In your answer, discuss: the theoretical basis of financial underwriting and its relationship to insurable interest doctrine; the practical limitations of income multiple frameworks in Nigeria’s predominantly informal economy; the AML/CFT obligations imposed on life insurers by the MLPPA 2022 and NAICOM guidelines, with specific reference to the underwriting process; and the organisational and operational reforms that would strengthen financial underwriting as an AML defence without creating an unacceptable market access barrier for legitimate applicants in the lower-income segment.

model.h: Thesis

Financial underwriting serves two distinct but complementary functions: it controls mortality risk by ensuring the sum assured is proportionate to genuine financial need, and it acts as a first line of AML/CFT defence by identifying suspicious applications before funds are placed into the life insurance system. Both functions are theoretically sound but practically limited in Nigeria's predominantly informal economy, creating a tension between rigour and market access that the industry has not yet adequately resolved.
Theoretical Basis: Risk Control Function

The financial underwriting rationale rests on insurable interest theory: a life policy should be proportionate to the financial loss the policyholder would suffer on the life assured's death. Over-insurance creates moral hazard; the beneficiary has more to gain from the insured's death than from their survival, potentially incentivising dangerous behaviour or fraudulent claims. Income multiples establish an objective proportionality test: an annual income of ₦5m supports a maximum sum assured of perhaps ₦75m at age 40 (15× multiple), amounts significantly above this threshold require documented justification.

The theoretical case is strong. In practice, the challenge is evidence: income multiples only work if income can be independently verified.
Limitations in Nigeria's Informal Economy

Nigeria's informal economy, estimated to account for 55–65% of GDP, is characterised by undocumented income, cash transactions, and the absence of formal payslips, tax returns, or audited accounts. For the typical Lagos market trader, Abuja contractor, or agricultural producer, declaring an annual income of ₦8m is plausible, unverifiable by any standard document, and routinely accepted on the basis of a bank statement showing turnover (not income).

Consequences of this limitation:
1. Income multiple frameworks are systematically less effective for the segment of the population that may have the most pressing protection need, informal sector workers with no employment-linked group life cover.
2. Refusal to underwrite without formal income documentation creates a de facto exclusion of informal sector workers from individual life assurance, a significant financial inclusion failure.
3. Conversely, accepting informal income declarations without verification creates openings for money laundering, placement of illicit funds through inflated income declarations.

The industry has not developed a credible alternative evidence framework for informal income verification (psychometric scoring, digital financial behaviour analysis, alternative data sources) that would enable rigorous financial underwriting without demanding documents that do not exist.
AML/CFT Obligations Under MLPPA 2022

The MLPPA 2022 imposes three core obligations that are relevant to the underwriting process:

1. Customer due diligence (CDD): Identification and verification of the applicant's identity (BVN, NIN, government-issued ID) and understanding of the nature of the insurance relationship before policy inception.

2. Enhanced due diligence (EDD): Triggered by high-value applications (NAICOM guidelines suggest ₦50m+ or any application with red flags), PEP status, or high-risk jurisdiction connections. EDD requires source of wealth evidence, deeper background investigation, and senior management sign-off.

3. Suspicious activity reporting: An application that cannot be satisfactorily explained (disproportionate sum assured, unexplained premium source, unusual beneficiary structure) must trigger a SAR to the NFIU, irrespective of whether the policy is ultimately declined.

The underwriting team is legally the first AML control point. A policy that proceeds past underwriting to inception has passed through the strongest filter in the customer journey, subsequent AML monitoring of an in-force policy is far less effective.
Reforms Required

1. Alternative income verification framework: NAICOM and the industry should develop a documented alternative evidence standard for informal sector income: 6 months of primary bank account statements showing deposit patterns; digital transaction history from mobile money platforms; CBN-registered cooperative membership records; utility payment history as a lifestyle marker.

2. Tiered AML thresholds: Acknowledge that not all applications present equal AML risk. A ₦5m individual life policy from a salaried Lagos civil servant presents minimal AML risk. The ₦50m policy from an undocumented cash business owner warrants full EDD. Calibrating the AML response to the actual risk level preserves market access for low-risk applicants.

3. Digital AML tools: BVN-linked adverse media screening, politically exposed person databases, and sanction list checking should be automated and embedded in the policy management system, reducing the time cost of AML compliance without compromising rigour.

4. Industry-shared fraud and AML intelligence: Nigerian life insurers should develop a shared database of declined applications (for financial underwriting and AML reasons) to prevent applicants from shopping for under-scrutinising insurers after being declined on legitimate grounds.

questions.stem: ‘The transformation from paper-based, examination-heavy underwriting to digital-first, triage-model underwriting is a commercial necessity for Nigerian life insurers seeking to grow their individual life book. However, this transformation carries material underwriting risk if it is not implemented within a rigorous actuarial and operational governance framework.’ Critically evaluate this proposition with reference to the Nigerian market. In your answer, discuss: the commercial drivers of underwriting digitalisation; the specific underwriting risks that arise from high Straight-Through Processing rates and reduced medical evidence collection; the role of the statutory actuary in monitoring underwriting adequacy under a digital-first model; and the safeguards that should be built into the governance framework to ensure that operational efficiency and risk control are maintained simultaneously.

model.h: Thesis

The proposition is correct on both counts. Digital underwriting transformation is commercially unavoidable, paper-based, examination-heavy processes cannot reach the volumes required for meaningful market growth. But the transformation carries genuine actuarial risk: faster decisions based on less evidence will, if poorly governed, produce an insured pool that is materially worse than the mortality table assumptions on which premiums are priced. The test of mature underwriting transformation is not speed; it is whether the mortality assumptions remain valid at scale.
Commercial Drivers of Underwriting Digitalisation

1. Distribution scale: The NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines 2025 have opened formal pathways for digital product distribution. A mobile-distributed life policy that requires a paper medical examination form creates immediate friction that kills conversion. The distribution model and the underwriting model must be aligned, digital distribution requires digital underwriting.

2. Cost efficiency: A paper-based underwriting process with individual medical examinations costs ₦15,000–₦40,000 per policy at modest sum assureds. For low-premium, low-sum-assured products targeted at the mass market, this cost exceeds the first-year premium, making the business model unviable. Straight-Through Processing (STP) reduces per-policy underwriting cost to near zero for standard risks.

3. Customer experience: The turnaround time from application to policy issuance in a digital STP model is minutes. In a paper model, it is weeks. Consumer willingness to persist through a long underwriting journey is low, particularly for the younger, digitally-native consumer segment that represents the best growth opportunity.
Underwriting Risks from High STP Rates

1. Anti-selection at scale: If the digital triage model directs 85% of applications to STP (instant acceptance) based on the declaration form alone, without any verification, those 85% include both genuinely standard risks and undisclosed substandard risks who have accurately calculated that declaring nothing generates automatic acceptance. At small volumes, this leakage is manageable. At the scale that digital distribution enables (100,000 policies per year), 1–2% of the STP book being materially undisclosed substandard risks could produce claims 15–20% above the pricing assumption.

2. Fraud escalation: STP removes the human review step that identifies implausible applications. Organised insurance fraud syndicates, who currently operate in Nigerian group life claims, will target digital life distribution as soon as volumes are large enough to make it worthwhile.

3. Portfolio composition drift: As the digital book grows rapidly, the insurer's mortality experience increasingly reflects the digital triage model's acceptance decisions, not the EFU table assumptions. If the digital triage model is more permissive than the EFU table assumes, the portfolio's true mortality rate will exceed the pricing assumption, and pricing will be inadequate.
The Statutory Actuary's Monitoring Role

Under NIIRA 2025, the Statutory Actuary has expanded responsibility for the adequacy of the insurer's pricing basis and the validity of its valuation assumptions. In the context of digital underwriting:

1. Annual mortality experience investigation: The Statutory Actuary must compare the actual mortality rate across the digital book against the assumed mortality rate in the pricing model. A consistent adverse variance (actual > assumed) is a signal that the triage model is admitting too many substandard risks.

2. Regular triage model review: The Statutory Actuary should review the STP model's acceptance criteria at least annually, assessing whether the declaration questions, the scoring rules, and the referral triggers remain appropriate for the portfolio's evolving risk profile.

3. Flagging to Board and NAICOM: If the mortality experience investigation reveals a material and worsening adverse experience on the digital book, the Statutory Actuary is obligated under NIIRA 2025 to report this to the Board and, if management does not address it adequately, to NAICOM.
Governance Safeguards

1. Triage model validation: Before deployment, the STP acceptance model must be validated by the Statutory Actuary against the pricing mortality assumption, confirming that the questions, scoring, and referral rules will, in practice, direct the risk distribution as assumed in pricing.

2. Claims-back analysis: Every declined or contested claim on a digital-origin policy should be reviewed against the STP decision: was the risk that led to the claim predictable from the information available at underwriting? Systematic patterns reveal triage model weaknesses.

3. Anti-fraud controls embedded at digital origination: BVN cross-referencing to detect multiple applications; velocity checks (same policyholder applying for multiple policies across different channels); beneficiary screening against known fraud indicators.

4. Escalation protocol: The triage model should have clear referral rules, any application that cannot be reliably classified as standard by the algorithm must be escalated to a human underwriter. The temptation to set the STP threshold at 95% acceptance to maximise conversion must be resisted; the actuarially appropriate acceptance rate is the governance test.
